title: Hungary's PM Moves to Amend Constitution, Oust President in Power Struggle
summary: Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar is taking the extraordinary step of amending the constitution to force out President Tamás Sulyok, escalating a political showdown just weeks after his landslide election victory. Magyar and his Tisza party hold a two-thirds parliamentary majority, giving them the power to rewrite the constitution and dismantle the autocratic system built by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán over 16 years. Magyar has repeatedly demanded Sulyok's resignation, calling him 'Orbán's puppet' and setting a May 31 deadline. After Sulyok refused during a Monday meeting at Sándor Palace, Magyar announced he would instruct lawmakers to begin the 'necessary procedures' to remove the president, a process he said would take about a month. While Hungary's presidency is largely ceremonial, the role includes signing legislation and referring bills to the constitutional court—powers that could obstruct Magyar's reform agenda. 'Hungary does not belong to Tamás Sulyok, nor to Viktor Orbán,' Magyar declared. 'The constitution states quite clearly that the president showcases the unity of the nation and guards the democratic functioning of the state.' He accused Sulyok of failing to uphold these duties by remaining silent when Orbán made dehumanizing remarks about opponents or when the previous government banned LGBTQ+ Pride events. Orbán's Fidesz party pushed back. Caucus leader Gergely Gulyás said in a video that 'in a constitutional democracy, it is not conceivable that a president is forcibly removed before his term of office ends,' warning that such a move would be a misuse of power. Sulyok's office has requested a legal assessment from the Venice Commission, a Council of Europe expert body. The conflict raises fundamental questions about the separation of powers in Hungary's young democracy. With both sides digging in, the coming weeks could redefine the country's political landscape.
why_it_matters: The standoff is a real-time test of whether a new democratic majority can use its power to dismantle the remnants of an autocratic system without itself undermining democratic norms. For young people across Europe, Hungary’s path could either set a model for reclaiming democracy or show how power struggles can erode trust in constitutions and courts.

background_read: Hungary, a central European country that was once part of the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc, became a democratic republic in 1989. Since 2010, Viktor Orbán (Hungary’s long-serving prime minister, known for his national-conservative and often illiberal policies) had dominated politics, changing the constitution and electoral laws to entrench Fidesz’s rule.

Péter Magyar’s Tisza party emerged as a new opposition force and won a stunning landslide in the latest election, giving it a two-thirds parliamentary supermajority. This is the same kind of majority that Orbán used for over a decade to amend the constitution at will.

The president of Hungary is largely a ceremonial figure, but the role still carries important duties: signing bills into law, representing the country internationally, and the power to refer legislation to the constitutional court for review. The president lives in Sándor Palace, the official residence in Budapest.

The Venice Commission is an advisory body of the Council of Europe made up of constitutional law experts. It is frequently asked to evaluate whether legal changes in member states comply with European democratic standards. Its opinion could influence how the European Union views the unfolding crisis.

The conflict reflects a deeper struggle over the separation of powers in a young democracy. Removing a sitting president by constitutional amendment, rather than through an impeachment process defined in the existing constitution, raises fundamental questions about the rule of law.

perspectives.description: Supporters of Magyar argue that the president, as an Orbán loyalist, is a leftover from a corrupt system. Removing him through constitutional means would clear the way for deeper reforms and undo 16 years of democratic backsliding. This could strengthen the rule of law and align Hungary more closely with European Union values.

Critics warn that using a supermajority to force out a president before his term ends sets a dangerous precedent. Even if the current president is compromised, the method—amending the constitution to sidestep ordinary impeachment—looks like the very playbook Orbán used to consolidate power. It could weaken the presidency permanently and remove an important check on the government.

The situation mirrors other post-authoritarian transitions where newly elected forces struggle with institutional remnants of the old regime. Historically, countries like Poland and South Africa faced similar dilemmas: how to replace compromised officials without destroying democratic guardrails. The Venice Commission’s opinion may offer a neutral legal benchmark, but the real political battle is about who defines what 'democratic functioning' means.

If the removal succeeds, Hungary could experience a rapid legislative overhaul, possibly restoring checks and balances lost under Orbán. However, the process might invite EU scrutiny and could trigger a constitutional crisis if the president refuses to step down. The outcome will influence how other European nations with strong executives treat their ceremonial heads of state, and may accelerate EU discussions on enforcing democratic standards.
